narrative:
The model predicted an 82% chance that you would fail the bar exam on your first attempt. Because this probability is so high, the admissions system automatically rejected your law school application.

The decision was driven primarily by three factors, ranked by importance. Your first-year and third-year class rankings were the strongest reasons for the negative outcome. Being in the bottom decile for grades in both Year 1 and Year 3 pushed the prediction strongly toward failure. These early academic results signaled to the model that you would likely struggle with the demands of law school and the bar exam. Your LSAT score was the third most influential factor, but it worked in the opposite direction: your score of 36 was only slightly below the average of accepted students (37.18), which gave the model a modest reason to expect you might pass.

Taken together, the model saw your consistently low class standing as far more important than your slightly below-average LSAT, resulting in the high risk of failure.

You should focus on strengthening your academic record. Retaking courses to improve your GPA, preparing intensively for a higher LSAT score, or gaining additional legal experience could help demonstrate stronger readiness for law school and the bar exam in a future application.
